That's the evidence a plan stands on. This clip is about the stage after it, where most plans I'm shown go wrong. A list of channels with "strategy" written at the top.

The cost is real, because a list of tactics gives you no basis for saying no to anything. The test I use is whether the line would still be true if every campaign changed. If it survives, it's strategy.

The situation analysis is the job to hand over. It comes back with three to five findings, each with its evidence, and a list of what it couldn't verify. A person still decides which findings matter.

clips.text: Strategy is the route. Who you'll target, how you'll position the brand against the alternatives, which channels carry the plan and which partners you'll work with. Tactics are the details of that route, what PR Smith describes as the marketing mix. The specific products, prices, places and promotions. I think that blur is where most plans go wrong, isn't it? A list of channels with "strategy" written at the top. Very often. And the cost is real, because a list of tactics gives you no basis for saying no to anything. The test I use is whether the line would still be true if every campaign changed. "Win cyclists who train indoors through the winter, through coaches and clubs rather than paid social." That survives a change of campaign, so it's strategy.

clips.text: Get AI on this: the situation pack. That's the one that eats the most time. Give it last year's results, your customer research and a list of your main competitors' websites, and it hands back a draft situation analysis with three to five findings, each with the evidence under it, and a list of what it couldn't verify. A person still decides which findings matter. Second, get AI on checking the plan you've already written. Paste in the draft plan and ask it to sort every line into the six SOSTAC stages. It hands back a table showing which stage each line belongs in, where tactics are sitting under strategy, and which objectives have no measure in control.
